Nobody talks much about term paper, so I would explain it more.
For the term paper, you will be given a list of topics first, then you will need to choose a topic on Canvas in 'groups' (That means you need to click into the group in which all people in that group would do the same topic in Canvas). If you fail to choose your favourite topic, you need to click into your second choice immediately. (You won't fail to choose a topic, but you may not be able to choose your favourite topic). You have around 2 weeks to complete your term paper.
⭐ I suggest you not to choose topics which are either too vague (e.g. origin of life) or too complicated (something you still don't know what is it after Google search), as you will struggle where to start your research. Usually in the list, the first few topic is very vague and the last few topics are very complicated. Try to choose the topics in the middle of the list (e.g. mitochondria, insulin, DNA mutations). They are relatively easy.
⚠️ However, the day of choosing topic is during the exam period, so you cannot start to write the paper until that day. Also, the deadline for the term paper is the day right after the last day of the exam period, so if you still have exam(s) on the last few days of the period, you may need to either do some research earlier or complete the term paper in 2-3 days.

comment_content:
Maybe I can briefly talk about what could happen in the exam. if you cannot read Chinese, then Google Translate could help.
Many questions require common sense or understanding of the term. For example, 停火在現代代表什麼意思? and the lecture notes only mentioned: "停火可以終止敵對而且实际上終止战争". You will feel that there are two impossible answers. option one: 雙方軍隊返回自己國家. option two:只要不簽訂和平條約, 就無法實現和平. so option two is selected by common sense.  Pay special attention to the term mentioned in States and Peaceful Settlement. 
Around 10 questions require an understanding of classical cases. eg. lotus case (船隻懸掛旗幟國家管轄權vs對在公海損害他船的外國船艦的管轄權, the case result: no exclusive jurisdiction, both countries have jurisdiction), the North Sea Continental Shelf Case (公約约束力的條件: 有些立法公約聲言是普遍性的，但成员方必須表明其接受約束的意向，但是他們可能不受約束),  Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries Case (由低潮點開始至外有十二英里的領海範圍, note that the case happened before UNCLOS but we still answer using this principle), the Cofu channel case (strict responsibility on potential damage)
10-13 questions about student presentation. Most of the topics have positions and conclusions, and most people use the principles of international law to prove them. What you should do is try to connect them, and the exam will gonna ask you about how they prove this. Note that each student topic has one question only. 但係我自己做嘅topic都唔肯定答案. One tip for preparing this is to listen to what the professor asks or answers.
10-13 questions about international institutions: 有d topic 係冇case study, 所以佢地會問國際機構嘅運作機制 or 條約. Eg. 國際海底管理局如何分配海床的利益, 國際原子能組織有關建立和管理核電廠的手則是否具備约束力, 赤道國家對《1975年波哥大聲明》聲稱靜態地理位置軌道是其領土的一部分, 1979年月球條約的內容. It does NOT mean that human rights institutions or UN institutions will NOT be examined.
History will be included but not many (around 4-5 questions). eg. Bynkershock於1702年表示國家擁有離岸至一定大炮射程的海域，例如三英里.  Grotius說正義戰爭
Last type of question: the professor's answers to any questions raised by students or the conclusion drawn by the professor during the lecture. One tip is to go to the lecture and ask a question, I found 3 questions in the exam that related to what I had asked.

Professor Julian Mcallister Groves is a veteran lecturer in HKUST, spending over 30 years in HKUST. As a native English speaker, his lectures should be understandable by everyone. Generally, his lecture videos follow the outline of the Powerpoint slides, though he is by no way a Powerpoint reader, so be sure to watch his videos in full!

comment_teaching:
Taking Contemporary Hong Kong Society gave me a deeper and more critical perspective on issues I used to take for granted. The course didn’t just provide facts — it challenged me to think about how Hong Kong’s social problems are connected to larger historical and structural forces.
One of the most memorable parts for me was the discussion on gender in Hong Kong. I had always assumed gender inequality was “less serious” here compared to other places, but through the readings and data, I realized how persistent workplace discrimination and cultural stereotypes still are. The debates on feminism in a local context made me reflect on how traditional values and modern ideals often clash.
The lecture on suicide and mental health was also very powerful. I appreciated that the course encouraged us to think sociologically about such a sensitive issue. Instead of framing suicide only as a personal tragedy, we examined the broader pressures — from housing, education, and family expectations — that shape people’s well-being. It reminded me that individual choices can’t be understood apart from social structures.
The historical dimension of the course also stood out. Learning about Hong Kong’s colonial past and post-1997 transformations gave me a better framework to understand today’s identity debates. It helped me see why issues like language, migration, and political participation continue to spark controversy.
Overall, I feel the course trained me to think critically about Hong Kong society by connecting theory to real-world problems. It also gave me tools — like gender theory, structural functionalism, and postcolonial perspectives — that I can use to analyze both current events and everyday life.

There are 4 non-cumulative quizzes, containing 24-26 MC and 1-2 short question(s). There are no classes, instead, you are engaged in 12 modules online. The modules contain lecture videos, readings (most of the modules) and movies (some of the modules). 
For the lecture videos, most of the questions (around 70%-80%) in the quizzes (except for quiz 4) are based on the content of the videos. Quiz 4, however, covers only around half of the questions related to the lecture videos since there are only 8 videos for module 9-12.
For the readings, questions about the readings are provided in the video and you have to answer them by reading the paper. Most of these questions have "correct" answers that are found within the readings. For the rest of them, you need to combine what you learnt in the lecture video and reading to explain your answer. 
It is unnecessary to read beyond the scope of these questions, as the instructor has not tested on material outside of this content. However, I recommend at least skimming through the abstract or introduction to grasp the core concepts of the readings.
For the movies, he will ask any content that the reporter or interviewee said. One of the MCs in a quiz has asked for the response of the neighbour of home husband, which only includes two sentences filmed in the movie. Therefore, I suggest watching the movies in details and take notes if possible. Besides, I had a concern whether the things I can see in the movies will be tested but luckily it has not been included in any quizzes.

If you've taken courses like SOSC1840 or others, this course would be rather easier to get a higher grade. For courses like SOSC1840, you have to remember the date of the law and details that you cannot find any relates in your life by rote. Comparing to other SOSC 1000-level courses, this course focuses ***more on understanding and some memorizing on phenomena that you can find relate to***. comment_content: It's a self-paced online course about contemporary Hong Kong society. It covers topics such as development, religion, inequality, ethnicity, gender, Hong Kong identity, family, youth, and migration. Each module includes short lecture videos, readings, documentaries, and discussion activities. There is no regular in-person attendance requirement, but you have to take at least three of the four quizzes (best 3 scores count).
comment_teaching: The short online lectures are convenient and generally well organized. The professor explains the main sociological concepts using examples from Hong Kong, while the readings and documentaries provide more detail. Since the course is self-paced, direct interaction is limited, although you can still communicate through Canvas discussions and email.
comment_grading:
The course has four closed-book quizzes, and you drop your lowest quiz score. The quizzes mainly consist of MCQs and one or two short-answer questions based on lectures, readings, documentaries, and discussion materials. There is also a personal reflection assignment that gives you an extra 1%. The quizzes can be quite detailed, so you need to study more than just the lecture summaries.
I studies like 2 or 3 days before the quiz for each one, mostly got above 1sd, got A.
comment_workload: The workload is manageable but can become heavy if the readings and documentaries are left until just before a quiz. The lecture videos are usually short, but each module also has readings and documentary content. There is no major group project or weekly graded homework, so the workload is flexible as long as you keep up with the modules.

comment_content:
hat explains Hong Kong’s phenomenal economic success? Why do a quarter of Hong Kong’s
population live below the poverty line? Why do women in Hong Kong outperform men in
education, but earn less money than men? Why do almost a thousand residents commit suicide
every year? What are the experiences of Hong Kong’s ethnically diverse minorities? How is Hong
Kong governed? What explains Hong Kong’s troubled political history? How do Hong Kong
residents see themselves in relation to the Chinese mainland? Why does Hong Kong have among
the highest divorce rates in the world? How is family life in Hong Kong changing?
The purpose of this course is to answer these questions, and more, by developing a sociological
understanding of Hong Kong society. The aim is not so much to compile facts and figures about
every conceivable aspect of Hong Kong, but to develop a sociological mindfulness with which to
understand it in new and helpful ways. We shall approach each topic by looking at the broad
questions and theories that sociologists use to understand modern life. We will then discuss their
relevance to Hong Kong and examine local studies. The course is, therefore, both an introduction
to sociological thinking and methods as well as an introduction to Hong Kong society.
The theme of the course is social change in Hong Kong from the post-war period. The focus is on
how industrialization, urbanization, globalization, and modernity affect our everyday lives,
institutions, relationships, and identities. The first two sections of the course will look at the
mechanics of these changes and selected social problems associated with them: the
transformation of community life, mental health, political, economic, and gender inequalities. The
final part will examine the implications of and responses to these problems: social movements for
democracy, experiences of discrimination, the emergence of distinct Hong Kong cultural identities,
and the search for intimacy, and family life.
